title: [Kubernetes] Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group
summary: We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standardCertified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions. Even so, every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support. A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from. What the working group will deliverThe charter sets out three deliverables: A specification of workload behavior for each Kubernetes minor version. A method for testing each requirement against a running workload. Upstream conformance tooling that implements those tests. The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers. The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn't yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them. However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification. The specification covers how a workload runs, and importantly not what it does. Consequently, application logic is out of scope of workload conformance. The binary won't retest anything Certified Kubernetes already covers, and it won't require a particular workload packaging format, or vendor tool like policy engine, security scanner, etc. How the work is organizedTwo Special Interest Groups (SIGs) are sponsors for the working group. SIG Architecture will own the specification and tooling through a subproject, which will be created once the first artifacts are proposed by the Working Group. SIG Apps will bring the application perspective. Whenever a requirement touches another Kubernetes SIG's area, such as node behavior or networking, the working group will initiate conversations with those SIGs as well. The working group is a forum where SIGs can get involved and shape the direction of Workload Conformance while the specification is being written. We're aiming for a stable first specification and working tests within two to three Kubernetes release cycles. Get involvedThe specification will and needs to be built from real examples, so we want to hear your experiences. If you run clusters, tell us how you assess workloads today and what broke during your last upgrade or maintenance window. If you maintain an application, tell us what it needs from the cluster and where the existing guidance left you guessing. Beyond examples, the work needs reviewers for proposed requirements and contributors to write the tests and tooling. When early versions of the tests are ready, we also want early testers to run the binary against your own workloads and tell us where the results differ between runs or environments. If a requirement touches your SIG's area, help us check its scope and the test behind it. And because the subproject will outlive the working group, we're also looking for people who want to maintain it for the long term. You can find us in #wg-workload-conformance on Kubernetes Slack (visit slack.k8s.io for an invitation) and on the mailing list. The working group meets every other Wednesday at 15:00 UTC. The Zoom link and the agenda are in the meeting notes. If you want to raise a topic, add it to the agenda. Joining the mailing list usually adds the meeting invite to your calendar. Thanks to everyone who reviewed and supported the working group proposal.

title: [Kubernetes] Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp
summary: You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect. In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?” The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort. This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example. Before you beginYou need a Kubernetes cluster with Kueue installed, a Headlamp installation, and the 0.1.0-alpha Kueue plugin. Your Kubernetes identity must be allowed to read the Kueue resources used in this article. The alpha release provides read-only views for Kueue v1beta2 Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues, ResourceFlavors, and Workloads. It does not add its own create, edit, stop, resume, or delete workflows. Headlamp still provides its standard YAML and resource actions where your permissions allow them. First, separate admission from Pod schedulingKueue and the Kubernetes scheduler answer different questions. Kueue admission: Should this Workload start now, considering queue policy, quota, ResourceFlavors, admission checks, and other waiting Workloads? Pod scheduling: After the Workload is admitted and the Job resumes, which nodes can run its Pods? That boundary changes the investigation. If the Workload is not admitted, stay in the Kueue section of Headlamp. If it is admitted but its Pods are still Pending, move to Headlamp's normal Job and Pod views and inspect scheduler events. Kueue admission architecture The Headlamp-first troubleshooting pathThe quickest investigation starts with the Workload, not with a shell. Tracing a pending Job through Headlamp Step 1: Open the Workloads viewIn Headlamp, open Kueue → Workloads. Select the namespace that contains the Job, then find the Workload created for it. Kueue creates a Workload to represent the resource request and admission state of a Job. In the alpha plugin, owner references are shown as Kind/name text but are not yet clickable. The Workload name normally contains the Job name, so the namespace filter and table search are the simplest ways to locate it. Before opening the detail page, the list already gives you a useful first scan: LocalQueue priority and priority class active state admitted state completion state a readable current status such as Admitted, Finished, or Inadmissible age If there is no matching Workload, check three things before going further: the selected namespace, whether the Job was submitted to a LocalQueue, and whether your Kubernetes account can list Workloads. The plugin performs permission checks and displays an access message when the current identity cannot read a resource. Step 2: Read status, conditions, and eventsOpen the Workload. Start with its current status and conditions, not with the full YAML. For admission troubleshooting, the most important condition types are QuotaReserved and Admitted. Admitted=True means Kueue has admitted the Workload. The Job can resume, so any remaining Pending Pods belong to the scheduling branch of the investigation. QuotaReserved=False with a reason such as Pending means Kueue has not reserved quota. The condition message explains what prevented the reservation. An Inadmissible status means the Workload currently cannot fit the available queue configuration. A missing covered resource, unsuitable ResourceFlavor, stopped queue, or admission check can all lead you here. For example, a condition message may report that Kueue could not assign a ResourceFlavor because the ClusterQueue has insufficient CPU quota. That message is the first real answer to “Why is my Job still pending?” The rest of the Headlamp journey explains the configuration behind it. Also check the Events section. Conditions describe the current state; events help show what recently changed or what Kueue attempted. Step 3: Compare the Workload's request with its assignmentStay on the Workload detail page and inspect the PodSets and resource requests. The plugin shows the requested Pod count, CPU, memory, and other resources that Kueue evaluates together. This matters because a Job with parallelism: 3 and a one-CPU request per Pod asks Kueue for three CPUs in total. Looking at only one Pod's template would underestimate the Workload. If quota has already been reserved, the same page also shows the assigned ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavors, and admitted resource usage. If those admission assignments are absent, the Workload has not reached that point yet. In our example, the Workload requests: three Pods three CPUs in total 600 MiB of memory in total The next question is where that request entered Kueue. Step 4: Follow the linked LocalQueueUse the LocalQueue link on the Workload detail page. A LocalQueue is the namespace-level entry point used by the Job. It connects namespaced Workloads to a cluster-scoped ClusterQueue. The LocalQueue page shows: its namespace and connected ClusterQueue stop policy and current status pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events related Workloads in the same namespace This page answers two practical questions: Did the Job enter the queue you expected, and is it the only Workload waiting there? If the LocalQueue is inactive or stopped, that may already explain the wait. If it is active, follow the linked ClusterQueue to inspect the capacity behind it. Step 5: Inspect ClusterQueue capacity and usageA ClusterQueue represents the cluster-level quota and admission policy available to one or more LocalQueues. On its Headlamp detail page, compare the Workload request with: covered resources nominal quota for each ResourceFlavor current reservations and usage borrowing and lending limits pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts queueing strategy and stop policy preemption, fair-sharing, flavor-fungibility, and admission-check settings Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events For the example in this article, the ClusterQueue provides a nominal quota of two CPUs and two Pod slots. The Workload asks for three of each. The condition message and the ClusterQueue page now tell the same story: the Workload does not fit, so Kueue leaves the Job suspended. This is an admission-capacity problem. It is not evidence that kube-scheduler failed to find a node. Step 6: Check ResourceFlavor and Cohort when neededQuota is not always a single pool. A ResourceFlavor can represent a class of compute through node labels, taints, tolerations, or topology settings. Use the ResourceFlavor link from the ClusterQueue when the condition mentions flavor assignment or when the Workload requires a particular hardware class, such as GPU nodes. If the ClusterQueue belongs to a Cohort, follow that link too. Cohorts let ClusterQueues share unused quota. The Headlamp page shows parent and child Cohorts, member ClusterQueues, referenced ResourceFlavors, resource groups, borrowing and lending limits, and fair-sharing information. These pages help answer a more subtle question: Is the Workload blocked because the queue has no quota of its own, because it cannot borrow enough, or because no suitable flavor can be assigned? What we learned without leaving HeadlampFor the sample pending Job, the UI gives us a complete explanation: The Workload is not admitted. Its QuotaReserved condition is false and the message points to insufficient quota. The Workload requests three CPUs and three Pod slots. Its LocalQueue is active and points to the expected ClusterQueue. The ClusterQueue provides only two CPUs and two Pod slots. Kueue therefore keeps the Job suspended until quota becomes available or the queue configuration changes. The important part is not that Headlamp invents a new status. It reads the same Kubernetes API objects as other clients, then places the related resources and human-readable values in one connected investigation. If the Workload is admitted, switch viewsSuppose the Workload detail page shows Admitted=True, but the application is still not running. Kueue has completed its part of the decision. Continue in Headlamp's standard Kubernetes views: Open Workloads → Jobs and inspect the Job state and events. Open Workloads → Pods and filter by the Job name or namespace. Select a Pending Pod and read its Events section. At this stage, look for scheduler concerns such as insufficient node capacity, node affinity, taints and tolerations, topology constraints, persistent-volume binding, or image-pull failures. This handoff is the most useful troubleshooting rule in the article: Not admitted: investigate Kueue resources in Headlamp. Admitted, but Pods are Pending: investigate Job, Pod, node, and scheduler information in Headlamp. A repeatable Headlamp checklistWhen the next Job does not start, use this short path: Open Kueue → Workloads and select the correct namespace. Find the Workload associated with the Job. Check the readable status, Admitted, and QuotaReserved conditions. Read the condition message and recent events. Compare PodSet resource requests with any admission assignments. Follow the LocalQueue link and confirm its status and ClusterQueue. Follow the ClusterQueue link and compare quota, reservations, usage, and policy. Inspect ResourceFlavor or Cohort details when the message points to flavor selection or shared quota. If admitted, move to Headlamp's Job and Pod views. What Headlamp replaces during this investigationThe plugin does not replace kubectl or kueuectl for scripts, exact object output, or changes. It replaces the repetitive UI-less navigation needed during an interactive investigation. Question Headlamp path Command-line equivalent Is the Workload admitted? Kueue → Workloads → status and conditions kubectl describe workload <workload-name> -n <namespace> Which LocalQueue did it enter? Workload → linked LocalQueue kubectl get localqueue <localqueue-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml Which ClusterQueue provides quota? LocalQueue → linked ClusterQueue kubectl get clusterqueue <clusterqueue-name> -o yaml Which flavor or shared quota matters? ClusterQueue → ResourceFlavor or Cohort kubectl get resourceflavor <flavor-name> -o yaml or kubectl get cohort <cohort-name> -o yaml What happened after admission? Workloads → Jobs and Pods → events kubectl describe job <job-name> -n <namespace> or kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> For scripts and GitOps workflows, the command line remains the right tool. For a person asking “why is this waiting?”, the linked Headlamp path is usually faster to read. Optional: reproduce the pending scenarioThe plugin repository includes sample Cohort, ClusterQueue, LocalQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Job manifests for local testing. Apply those examples to a cluster where Kueue is installed, then open the Kueue section in Headlamp. To reproduce the specific quota mismatch used in this article, configure a ClusterQueue with two CPUs and two Pod slots, then submit a three-Pod Job that requests one CPU per Pod. The Job enters its LocalQueue, Kueue creates a Workload, and the Workload remains pending because the combined request is larger than the available quota. Keeping this setup separate from the main walkthrough is intentional: once the resources exist, the investigation itself should happen in Headlamp. Current alpha limitationsThe 0.1.0-alpha release is an initial read-only view of the Kueue admission path. The plugin does not add its own create, edit, pause, resume, or delete flows. Workload owner references are displayed as text and are not currently navigable. The UI depends on the Kubernetes permissions of the identity used by Headlamp. Metrics and a visual relationship map are possible follow-up areas rather than features of this release. These limits are useful to state clearly: the plugin's current purpose is to make admission state and resource relationships easier to inspect. Developed during LFX MentorshipThe plugin was developed during CNCF LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 2 using TypeScript, React, Kubernetes APIs, and Headlamp's plugin system. Utkarsh Raj implemented the plugin with guidance and review from René Dudfield (@illume) and Kevin Hannon (@kannon92). Feedback from the Headlamp and Kueue communities shaped the resource views, status presentation, navigation, documentation, tests, and first alpha release. Try it and share feedbackExplore the plugin source and README, read the 0.1.0-alpha release documentation, or share feedback in the release issue. If a pending Workload is still difficult to explain after following the Headlamp path, that is exactly the kind of feedback that can improve the plugin.

title: [Cloudflare] Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
summary: Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026.Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States.These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year.Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project, Cloudflare for Campaigns, and Project Galileo. Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,400 election-related websites during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, including those belonging to state and local governments, candidates, political parties, voting-rights advocates, journalists, and civil society groups.Cloudflare launched its first election protection program in 2016 after widespread reports of cyberattacks targeting the U.S. elections. A decade later, it is remarkable to see how far governments and campaigns have come in securing their digital infrastructure. We are proud to help protect democratic institutions and are encouraged that cyberattacks were once again not a disruptive factor in 2026.In this post, we examine traffic and attacks observed against those organizations on Election Day, analyze the most common types of attacks of the 2026 cycle, and provide recommendations based on those findings.Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacksOrdinary user traffic to state and local government election websites was higher on Election Day (November 3) than any other day in 2026. Traffic to those sites increased to approximately 602 million requests, up from 130 million on November 1. By comparison, traffic across the rest of Cloudflare’s global network rose by only 12% over the same period.State and local government election websites provide authoritative information to voters on how to register, where to vote, and who won. Because of their critical role, these platforms are often targeted by those seeking to suppress voter turnout, disrupt the reporting of results, or steal sensitive information.On Election Day itself, Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack across any of its 1,400 election-related websites. The only significant DDoS attack occurred on November 2, targeting a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in California and totaled 520,000 requests. By comparison, the Moldovan Election Commission experienced more than 898 million malicious requests in a single 12-hour period on their Election Day in 2025, with attacks peaking at 324,333 requests per second.Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycleWebsite vulnerability scans were by far the most common attack observed by Cloudflare in the 2026 U.S. election cycle. In the 12 months leading up to the election, Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks on government election websites alone.Website vulnerability attacks exploit outdated or vulnerable website code to gain access to internal systems and data. For example, cross-site scripting attacks inject malicious code into web pages in order to capture administrator credentials or deface site content. SQL injection manipulates database queries allowing attackers to potentially extract voter records or alter data.Phishing and other malicious emails targeting political campaigns protected by the company occurred at rates consistent with Cloudflare's broader network, but showed signs of sophistication. In the 90 days leading up to the election, 3.9% of emails sent to organizations participating in Cloudflare for Campaigns were identified as malicious, closely tracking the 4.8 percent baseline across other Cloudflare customers. However, nearly 42% of those malicious emails managed to bypass basic email authentication checks, such as verifying sender identity or preventing in-transit tampering. These threats were nonetheless identified by Cloudflare’s advanced phishing detection tools.Although website vulnerabilities were the most common attack overall, for journalism and election-related civil society organizations, DDoS was the most common. Over the same 12-month period, Cloudflare mitigated over 10.8 billion DDoS requests targeting these groups. The largest single attack occurred on September 10, 2026, hitting a U.S.-based news organization with 3.04 billion requests. This pattern is consistent with Cloudflare research released earlier this year, which found that among all Project Galileo entities in 120 countries, DDoS were by far the most common attack seen, accounting for 81% of all attacks.PHP vulnerabilityOn October 21, security researchers disclosed serious vulnerabilities (known as php2shell) in PHP, an open source back-end programming language used by 70% of the world's websites. The flaws reportedly could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Cloudflare deployed Web Application Firewall (WAF) protections for all customers, prior to public disclosure of the vulnerability.On October 22, Cloudflare's PHP defense was triggered more than 9,000 times on a state government election website in the Western U.S. This attack was only detected on one election-related site and appears to have been an isolated incident rather than part of a broader trend.RecommendationsCloudflare research consistently shows that individuals and organizations participating in democratic elections face significant risk of cyberattack. Data gathered during the 2026 U.S. midterm election suggests those attacks continue to evolve, occur throughout an election cycle and not only on Election Day, and can vary depending on the type of organization targeted.Based on the recent cyberattack trends in the 2026 U.S. midterms and other elections, we make the following recommendations: Prepare for surges in user traffic. Legitimate voter interest can create traffic spikes that overwhelm unprepared infrastructure and make essential election websites inaccessible. Organizations should prepare scalable, efficient infrastructure to handle Election Day traffic increases without straining budgets or staff. Maintain security protections year-round, not just on Election Day. Cyberattacks targeting democratic institutions occur across the entire election cycle, not just around voting windows. Defensive postures must remain active continuously rather than treated as a short-term, seasonal measure.Deploy automated defenses to counter rapid threats. AI has made it easier for attackers to find and exploit new vulnerabilities. Organizations should implement security services that update automatically, like managed rules, to ensure new protections deploy by default.Ensuring voters have access to reliable information about elections not only helps encourage participation and deliver timely, accurate results, but also protects voter confidence in the democratic process itself. As more officials, more institutions, and the public increasingly rely on the Internet for those services, keeping that digital infrastructure stable, secure, and accessible becomes an essential civic priority.State and local election offices, political campaigns, party organizations, journalists, and voting rights groups in need of cybersecurity services can access them from Cloudflare at no cost. Visit the Athenian Project (for state and local election websites), Cloudflare for Campaigns (for political campaigns), or Project Galileo (for civil society, democracy, and journalism organizations) to learn more about eligibility and sign up today.

title: [Docker] Meet the New Docker: Built to Run on Trust
summary: Evolving an iconic brand for the agentic era Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change. Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago. But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents? That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a new Docker. A new Docker, but a familiar story. We’ve been here before Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment. Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker. Together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.” Today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers. What isn’t changing Let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it. The qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us. On the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way. Containers weren’t designed for agents Agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors. Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control. Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe. Run on trust In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the new Docker is all about trust. Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves. Trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise. Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in. Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not. A whale of an evolution As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a new day for Docker. Something that says and shows, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore. Something big. Something, dare I say, whale sized. I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby. If you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation company, Motto, we landed on a new Moby for the new Docker. Watch Moby’s transformation here: In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a new era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby. Come take a look around We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think. Wherever this new era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

title: [Docker] Give sandboxed agents live web access with the Firecrawl kit for Docker Sandboxes
summary: Sandboxed agents cannot read the web A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy. The same controls keep the agent from opening a docs page, reading a changelog, or looking up an API that shipped after its training cutoff, so it writes code against the version it remembers. The usual fix is to widen the allowlist until the agent can fetch anything, which hands back most of what the sandbox took away. The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown. In this post, you’ll learn: How the Firecrawl sandbox kit plugs into a sandbox you already run How to install the sandbox kit and give your agent its first live-web task How to check that the SDK, the API key, and the network rule all work What the sandbox kit can’t do yet, and what new work it makes possible for your agent Why a kit The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a new sandbox. Its descriptor, firecrawl/firecrawl.yaml, declares four typed capabilities: An install step (lifecycle@1). It installs the Firecrawl Python SDK, firecrawl-py, pinned to 4.44.0, as the agent user, and fails sandbox creation if the install or import check fails. A credential (credential@1). It requests a proxy-managed firecrawl API key. Inside the sandbox, FIRECRAWL_API_KEY holds the placeholder proxy-managed; the proxy swaps in the real key on requests to api.firecrawl.dev, so the key never enters the image or the sandbox. Network permissions (network-policy@1), split by phase. The install step may reach pypi.org and files.pythonhosted.org; at runtime the agent may reach api.firecrawl.dev. Agent instructions (agent-context@1). A context file tells the agent the capability exists, how to call it, and which limits come from the sandbox. The workload indexes it from its own AGENTS.md. The kit adds to the sandbox’s allowlist and does not narrow it, so everything else is set by your global sbx policy. Docker’s balanced preset allows package registries, GitHub, and a curated list of vendor domains, and returns a 403 for general websites, including most documentation sites, so Firecrawl is the agent’s route to those. Under deny-all, it is the agent’s only web host. Kits are experimental and in Early Access, so the kit format and sbx commands may change. The steps below are current for October 2026; the repository README carries the latest. The workflow Prerequisites The sbx CLI, version 0.46 or later, signed in with sbx login. On macOS: brew trust docker/tap && brew install docker/tap/sbx. Docker Desktop is not required. A global network policy, set once with sbx policy init balanced. Without it, no sandbox starts. A Firecrawl API key (fc-...) from firecrawl.dev/app/api-keys. A workload to add the kit to. This walkthrough uses Docker’s shell workload, docker/sbx-kit-shell, with the Claude Code mixin, docker/sbx-kit-claude-mixin. Other workloads and agent mixins are on Docker Hub. Kit: docker.io/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl:1.0.0 on Docker Hub, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Source: github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl-docker-sandbox. 1. Store the key once on the host. The command prompts for the key. Service secrets are global by default, so every sandbox that requests the firecrawl service can use it once you approve. The kit never sees the value; the proxy injects it at request time. sbx secret set firecrawl sbx secret ls 2. Start a sandbox with the kit. The kit is an ordinary OCI image with its descriptor in the manifest, so a version tag is all you need. Each --kit adds a mixin to the workload, and the trailing . mounts your project directory. sbx run docker/sbx-kit-shell:1.0.0 \ --kit docker/sbx-kit-claude-mixin:2.1.285 \ --kit docker.io/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl:1.0.0 . On the first run, sbx asks you to approve sending the firecrawl credential to api.firecrawl.dev. Accept the defaults. The credential is required: with no secret stored, sbx refuses to create the sandbox instead of letting the agent hit a 401 mid-task. A detached or CI run cannot answer the approval prompt, so approve interactively once or write the binding to ~/.config/sbx/credentials.yaml first. 3. Give the agent a task that needs the live web. Documentation sites are blocked under balanced, so this one has to go through Firecrawl. Read <https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/changelog/> and list what changed in the latest Pydantic release. Quote the page, don't answer from memory. The kit’s instructions tell the agent to scrape blocked hosts through Firecrawl, so it calls fc.scrape(...) unprompted. Its response, trimmed: The most recent release listed on the changelog is v2.13.4 (2026-05-06). I fetched the page live through Firecrawl. Quoted from the page: > ## v2.13.4 (2026-05-06) > ### What's Changed > #### Packaging > - Bump libc from 0.2.155 to 0.2.185 by @Viicos in #13109 > - Adapt `pydantic-core` linker flags on macOS by @washingtoneg and @Viicos in #13147 > #### Fixes > - Preserve `RootModel` core metadata by @Viicos in #13129 It's a small patch release with no new features. 4. Verify each layer. In the same session, ! runs shell commands inside the sandbox. !python3 -c "import firecrawl, importlib.metadata as m; print('firecrawl-py', m.version('firecrawl-py'))" Expected: firecrawl-py 4.44.0. !env | grep FIRECRAWL_API_KEY Expected: FIRECRAWL_API_KEY=proxy-managed. A real fc-... value here means the key came from somewhere other than the kit. !python3 - <<'PY' from firecrawl import Firecrawl fc = Firecrawl() doc = fc.scrape("<https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/changelog/>", formats=) print(doc.markdown) PY Expected: the page as markdown, starting with # Changelog and the latest version heading. The same URL returns a 403 to curl from inside the sandbox, so output here proves the SDK, the credential, and the network rule at once. The kit also describes itself inside the sandbox. This prints the published descriptor, and the agent instructions sit next to it as firecrawl-context.md: !cat /usr/share/sandbox/kit/firecrawl/kit.yaml Running from source. To review or modify the kit before you run it, clone the repository and point --kit at the firecrawl/ directory; sbx builds source kits on demand: git clone <https://github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl-docker-sandbox.git> sbx run docker/sbx-kit-shell:1.0.0 --kit ./firecrawl-docker-sandbox/firecrawl . Known limitations Under balanced, general websites return a proxy 403 to curl, so a URL found in a scrape result has to be scraped through Firecrawl too. Screenshot and other media formats return links on Firecrawl’s storage host, which the allowlist does not include, so those files cannot be downloaded inside the sandbox. Under organization governance, managed policy overrides the kit’s allow rule, and scrapes fail with a proxy-side 403 until the organization allows api.firecrawl.dev. An HTTP 402 means the Firecrawl account is out of credits; the agent is told to stop rather than retry. What this unlocks With the kit installed, the agent can look things up on the web while it works. The sandbox only needs to talk to one new address, api.firecrawl.dev, and Firecrawl fetches the pages for it. This matters because the default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites. Without the kit, you’d have to allow each site one by one, and every new site you allow makes the sandbox a little less locked down. Without the kit, you had a choice to make. The default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites, so you could either leave the agent working from what it remembered, or allow sites one by one and loosen the sandbox a little each time. The kit avoids that choice. Your Firecrawl API key stays on your machine, behind the proxy, and the agent still reads the web as it is today. Here’s what the agent can do: Code against the current API, not the remembered one. Before calling a library or SaaS API, the agent scrapes its reference page and changelog. It uses today’s parameter names and spots deprecations that shipped after its training cutoff. Upgrade dependencies with the release notes in hand. Asked to bump a package, the agent reads the release notes for every version in between, lists the breaking changes, and edits the code to match before running the tests. Load a vendor’s docs into context. For a new integration, the agent crawls the relevant section of the vendor’s docs and gets it back as markdown, so it can work from the whole guide rather than one page. Research an error it can’t explain. When a build or test fails with an unfamiliar message, the agent searches for it, reads the matching GitHub issue or forum thread, and applies the documented fix or workaround. Cite its sources. Because every answer comes from a fetched page, the agent can quote the text and link the URL it used, so you can check its work. The result is fewer made-up APIs, fewer failed upgrades, and less time spent correcting an agent that was confidently out of date. Where the kit comes from The kit is published under the firecrawl organization on Docker Hub as firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl, with source, changelog, and CI on GitHub under Apache-2.0. The SDK pin is verified against PyPI’s package hashes at install time, and every release passes Docker’s kit-tck conformance suite in CI. Review the descriptor and allowlist before running it, as with any kit. Try it Pull the kit from Docker Hub: hub.docker.com/r/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl. Issues and feature requests go to the GitHub repository.

title: [GitLab] The recommended GitLab configuration for agentic engineering
summary: Agents keep getting better at more than drafting code. Teams already use them to move work through review, repair pipelines, and push changes toward merge. That speed only helps if every change is based on the software lifecycle context that lives in a unified platform and still passes the same gates your organization trusts. Without it, context, controls, and evidence fragment across people and tools into a shadow software factory.Identity, policy, CI pipelines, security, approvals, and audits have to travel with the change from plan through merge and into production. Your coding harness and GitLab Duo Agent Platform are built to work in tandem, so coding agents can move quickly while GitLab certifies their work on the way to production.Software teams get to use different coding tools and agents they prefer, while their GitLab instance makes sure that every change is safe to ship. GitLab stays cloud-neutral, model-neutral, and agent-neutral, so you keep the harnesses, models, and deployment path that fit your organization.Let us show you how to configure your agentic engineering environment to drive greater automation throughout your workflow. You stay in the harness you already use and connect to GitLab Duo Agent Platform once with a skill. Longer, repository-aware workflows run on GitLab, and every merge request still hits the same reviews, pipelines, scans, and approval policies.In this article, we will focus on Claude Code as the local harness because that’s what we see most of our customers using but this same flow can apply to the local harness of your choosing, including Duo CLI.How to configure your agentic engineering environmentIf you already do most of your coding in a local harness, keep working there and wire it to GitLab Duo Agent Platform. From the terminal, you can direct lifecycle work to agentic workflows that run inside GitLab:Picking up an issue and opening a merge requestReviewing every MR as it landsResolving merge conflictsRepairing a pipeline that just failedWith GitLab Ultimate, triaging and fixing security findings once code landsClaude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and others become the place from where you direct that work.Part 1 is the setup:Install the GitLab Duo setup skill, ask Claude Code to run it, and it sets up your whole top-level group with the necessary settings, the flows, an automation in every project, and the MCP connection.Part 2 walks through four workflows:You can try them as soon as the setup is done, each driven from Claude Code:Find an issue assigned to you and hand it to the Developer flow.Get automated code reviews on your merge requests, act on the findings without leaving your harness, and resolve any conflicts that pop up.Use an automation to fix a failed pipeline.On Ultimate, triage and fix security findings with the security flows.When you want an even tighter loop:The MR followup skill guides your local harness through the steps above even faster. The skill helps local agents monitor progress on the repo-side and take actions on your behalf to speed things along.What you get from the combined path:Move faster: Automatic review, pipeline repair, and (on Ultimate) security triage keep changes moving without leaving your harness.Build trust: The same engineering and security standards apply to every MR, with oversight and an audit trail in GitLab.Reduce complexity: Automate the handoff between your harness and GitLab so lifecycle work shares one context, one set of gates, and one audit trail.What you need before you start:A GitLab.com top-level group with GitLab Credits (Premium and Ultimate groups get access to promotional free credits each month for each user). The security workflow in Use Case 4 requires Ultimate licensing for your GitLab instance.A project in that group with a pipeline, a few open issues, and an open merge request or two, so the workflows have something to act on.The Owner role on the top-level group, so the skill can set up the whole group. title: [Engineering at Meta] Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Building a Template-Driven ML Ecosystem
summary: As ML ecosystems grow to a large number of production models, the bottleneck is no longer inventing new techniques to improve these models, but rather shipping them reliably and efficiently across a fragmented model space, creating a rising tide that lifts all the boats. At Meta, we built a template-driven approach that standardizes model design into a small set of reusable and composable building blocks, turning model iteration from a per-model problem into a shared systems problem. Over the last two years, this approach reduced per-model engineering time by 92%, shipped 5000+ technique-model combinations, improved offline model quality by 0.63% on average at neutral serving capacity, and delivered 0.86% cumulative online lift covering 70% of models by count. This work is fully detailed in our paper, “Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Template-Driven ML Development for Large Model Ecosystems.” Meta’s ads ranking systems process billions of daily requests across a diverse array of products and optimization goals, served by a large number of production models. At that scale, the main challenge in improving user relevance and advertiser value has shifted from inventing new techniques to propagating them. Every high-impact idea needs to reach every model it applies to, and adapting it one model at a time does not scale with the fleet. Fragmentation compounds quickly in large-scale ML systems. A new architecture lands on one model, but bringing it to every corner of the ecosystem may take years. A platform migration works for one family of models, but breaks on a long tail of specialized configurations. A tuning insight improves one model, but says little about the next one because the underlying setup is too different. Over time, propagation becomes more difficult than the innovation itself. Meta’s ads ranking ecosystem ran into this exact problem. As the number of production models grew with the diversity of ads optimization objectives, so did the diversity of architectures, features, training settings, serving constraints, and platform-specific logic. That diversity gave teams flexibility, but it also created three systemic problems: high engineering cost to ship new ideas broadly, high reliability cost from an explosion of corner cases, and low predictability when trying to estimate the ecosystem-wide impact of a change. The deeper issue is that fragmentation creates an unfavorable scaling law for engineering itself. If each idea must be evaluated and adapted per model, the work grows linearly with the number of models. That is manageable early on, but becomes a serious bottleneck when you have a large number of models. Fragmentation also weakens automation. AutoML and optimization systems work best in a structured space, but when every model has a different shape, the highest-potential techniques reach only a subset of models. Our answer was not to add another layer of automation on top of this complexity. Instead, we started by reducing the complexity itself. We did this by introducing Standard Model Templates (SMT), an approach that standardizes model design into a curated set of reusable templates. Figure 1: Before SMT, each technique was tuned by hand on each model, and the combinations to try grew exponentially. With SMT, multi-model optimization tunes techniques once across representative models, and the ones that generalize go into the next template version. A Template-Driven Foundation A template is an opinionated, minimal model setup built from shared components such as architecture choices, feature logic, training settings, and serving configs. Instead of maintaining every production model as a largely independent design, we group similar models around a smaller number of standard templates. Model-specific logic still exists where necessary, but the common parts are explicitly represented and shared. In practice, we use a small set of templates that cover major ranking and retrieval patterns across different model sizes. These templates package reusable components for feature selection, feature interaction, model parallelism, training configuration, and hardware-aware serving. This changes the operating model in an important way. Instead of evaluating a new idea independently on every model, we can evaluate it on a much smaller set of representative templates and then propagate it to the model groups that use them. In other words, we shift from per-model iteration to template-level iteration. That gives us three main advantages. Reduced propagation complexity: A shared template lets one implementation serve many downstream models, which lowers the cost of shipping new ideas at scale. Improved reliability: When there are fewer unique model setups, it becomes practical to build stronger validation, better guardrails, and more transferable debugging workflows. Problems such as training instability or serving regressions become easier to reason about because they occur within a shared template structure rather than an unbounded configuration space. Improved predictability: When models in a group share a common template, performance on representative models becomes a much better signal for the rest of the group. That makes ecosystem-level planning more grounded and less assumption-driven. Over time, this template-driven approach became more than a standardization effort. It became the foundation for a broader ML development system. Figure 2: The SMT development loop (left) and the layered architecture inside each template (right). Techniques are tuned once across representative models, added to a new template version, and rolled out to every model built on it. SMTs: From Standardization to Scalable Technique Transfer The shift to SMTs unlocked a more ambitious capability — the ability to optimize the entire ecosystem as a single, cohesive unit. Rather than managing a fleet of independent models, we began treating the landscape as a shared innovation surface. Instead of propagating individual techniques one by one, we transfer proven holistic model designs from strong source models into target model families through a shared template layer. This matters because many gains come from interactions between architectural choices, scaling decisions, and training strategies, not from isolated components applied independently. Over the last 2 years, this approach reduced per-model engineering time by 92%, shipped 5000+ technique-model combinations across our large diverse fleet of models , while improving offline model quality by 0.63% on average at neutral serving capacity, and delivered 0.86% cumulative online lift. More importantly, it challenged a common assumption that diverse optimization goals require highly diversified model designs. In many cases, a well-designed shared template can generalize much further than expected. We also found that once model structure is standardized, scaling decisions become more reusable. Rather than rediscovering cost-performance trade-offs separately for every model, we can learn them in template space and apply them more broadly. This led to scaling-law-based optimization workflows that make resource allocation more principled and less ad hoc. Multi-Model Optimization We use multi-model optimization to make template iteration rigorous. This process evaluates candidate techniques across representative models and searches for configurations that improve aggregate performance while limiting regressions. A technique with a strong average gain but frequent regressions is difficult to ship across a large fleet. Consistency is as important as peak improvement for production-scale propagation. Multi-model optimization considers both aggregate performance and regression rate when deciding whether a technique is ready for integration. After optimization, candidate techniques are validated on held-out models to check whether gains transfer beyond the representative set. Techniques that pass are integrated into the next template version. Over the last two years, we shipped 80 new ML techniques through this workflow. The result is compounding. Every model that adopts a mature template inherits a history of generalized improvements rather than starting from an isolated baseline. Why SMT Matters for Agentic ML Systems Agentic model building often envisions a single end-to-end agent exploring a large design space with access to tools, training pipelines, and evaluation results. In practice, that approach runs into a familiar problem: The search space is too unconstrained. Without strong priors, an agent spends too much effort exploring unproductive regions, recovering from avoidable failures, or proposing changes that are difficult to explain and harder to ship. SMT helps solve that problem because they encode known-good design patterns, which gives agents a structured starting point, a bounded search space, and a quality floor. Instead of treating model building as free-form search, we can decompose it into specialized subproblems. At Meta, SMTs are also the foundation for our multi-agent approach to model building. Templates provide the structure, and agents provide adaptive exploration and automation. At the template level, agents help build, evaluate, and improve the templates themselves. They propose optimization ideas based on proven techniques, launch experiments across representative models, diagnose failures, and iterate over multiple rounds, which helps manage the multi-day loops that template development requires. Agents can also take on harder work such as migrating models to new hardware platforms. A technique validated this way reaches every model built from that template, at a fraction of the compute it would take to adapt each model separately. We cover this in more detail in our post, How Meta Uses AI Agents to Scale ML Techniques Across Ads Ranking Models. Lessons Learned and the Road Ahead for SMTs Propagating ML innovations to improve models is often the main scaling challenge in large ML ecosystems. SMTs succeed because automation gets more powerful as the underlying system becomes more structured. Template-driven development did not just make the ecosystem easier for humans to operate. It also made it easier for optimization systems, scaling workflows, and agents to reason effectively. But standardization only works if it is opinionated enough to remove unnecessary diversity, while still preserving the limited flexibility that matters. A template system that tries to accommodate every historical edge case will eventually recreate the fragmentation it was meant to solve. There is more work to do in improving template coverage, strengthening scaling-law-based optimization, and moving toward fully end-to-end agentic workflows — including agentic template building, model generation, online evaluation, and continuous optimization from online signals. We also need to make these workflows more reliable and more explainable. But the central idea has held up. If you want to scale ML innovation across a large ecosystem, you need to standardize the surface on which that innovation lands. In other words, designing once and deploying at scale is not just an efficiency tactic; it is an architectural choice about how to make a large ML ecosystem learn faster. Read the Paper “Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Template-Driven ML Development for Large Model Ecosystems.” Acknowledgements Aayush Aggarwal, Saurabh Aggarwal, Anuj Bindal, Nakul Camasamudram, Shouyuan Chen, Wenlin Chen, Kevin De Angeli, Jason Flaks, Luc Kien Hang, Rupinder Khandpur, Santanu Kolay, Nhat Le, Swamy Muddu, Sandeep Pandey, Dhiraj Parashar, Akshay Pardeshi, Jingzheng Qin, Shah Rahman, Shiblee Sadik, Munaf Sahaf, Vibha Sinha, Saied Tahaghoghi, Terry Tang, Alireza Vahdatpour, Fangjing Wu, Haoyu Wu, Wendan Yan, and Chang Yang. title: [Engineering at Meta] Your Algorithm: Giving People More Ways to Personalize Facebook Recommendations
summary: Your algorithm is a suite of AI-powered tools that makes Facebook recommendations more transparent and steerable, with a single editable view of the interests that shape Feed and Reels. We’re sharing how Your algorithm turns people’s natural language preferences into responsive recommendations, and how LLMs are tailored to specific tasks within the system. Traditionally, the recommendation systems behind what people see on Facebook have learned from implicit engagement signals. While this allows them to scale well, it also means they adapt slowly and capture little nuance. But what if people could interact directly with the algorithms that rank and recommend what they see to instantly make their recommendations more personal and customized? Your algorithm is an end-to-end system that addresses the limitations of adaptability and nuance in recommendations. This new suite of AI-powered tools lets people on Facebook state, in their own words, what they want to see in their Feed and Reels. By tasking a collection of large language models (LLMs) with understanding, storing, and tracking people’s stated preferences along with their user behavior, we’ve created a recommendation system that responds to people’s preferences and adjusts the content they see. An Overview of the Your Algorithm System Architecture The Your algorithm page has three parts (Figure 1): At the top, a one-sentence Lately Summary that describes recent viewing activity. Below it are two lists: “Interested In,” prefilled with interests inferred from past activity. “Not Interested In,” capturing topics the user has explicitly marked as not interested, or has X-ed out or hidden on Facebook. People can use the interface to add interests (using natural language), move them between lists, or remove them. Every change applies responsively to both Feed and Reels, and will further update as the person gives feedback on individual posts. Figure 1: The Your algorithm page. Your algorithm system has several components that cover the full lifecycle of a preference, from inferring and validating it to applying it in ranking and delivery (Figure 2). Profile generation builds the initial interest profile. Preference management validates each change, enriches it with the signals ranking needs, and saves it to a single store that both Feed and Reels read, ensuring that the preferences shown on the page are the same ones used in ranking. Ranking applies the “Interested In” and “Not Interested In” lists throughout the funnel. Delivery optimization helps each change take effect more responsively. Figure 2: An overview of the Your algorithm system. From Preferences Into Recommendations Turning a stated preference into recommendations poses three distinct problems. An interest added to Interested In needs to deliver relevant content quickly, without crowding out everything else. An interest added to Not Interested In needs to hold reliably, even though topics are fuzzy and any single filter misses some matches. And both need to take effect responsively, even when the next recommendations were cached before the change. Your algorithm addresses each problem with dedicated logic across the recommendation funnel, from retrieval through reranking to the device (Figure 3). Interested In: Surfacing New Interests Without Flooding Each interest in Interested In drives four dedicated retrieval sources. Two find matching content directly (through search and through clusters of closely related topics), and two extend reach through the content graph and item-to-item similarity. Retrieving explicitly for each interest ensures enough relevant candidates for downstream ranking. This is important because, without it, content about a brand-new interest might never enter the ranking pipeline at all. Candidates that pass a relevance check, which compares the meaning of the interest with each candidate, receive a promotion in late-stage ranking so they can compete alongside other content. A control layer in reranking then determines where they appear. Responsiveness alone is not the goal. Our approach emphasizes balance over volume: A new interest should show up, not take over. The control layer spaces out recommendations for the same interest and caps each interest’s daily contribution. Retrieval also fetches candidates for only one interest per request, so every interest gets a turn. New interests receive extra weight for a limited period. After that, the recommendation system learns from how people engage with that content. Not Interested In: Layered Filtering at Every Stage Interests in Not Interested In are enforced at several stages based on different signals to achieve high precision and recall. During ranking, the same embedding-based comparison used in the relevance check removes candidates too close to an interest in Not Interested In, and demotion rules push down near matches. After ranking, the LLM reranker reviews the final list. On the device, cache invalidation, described below, removes matching candidates that are already queued for display. Not every entry in Not Interested In is about a topic. Quality-related requests, such as reducing AI-generated or sexually suggestive content, map to dedicated demotion signals rather than topic matching. When a request names a creator, that creator’s content is filtered out directly. Responsiveness Optimization Even with ranking tuned to respond to preferences, there is still room to improve how responsively a change reaches what people see. Content for a new preference is not picked up until the next fetch request, and content already cached on the device was ranked before the preference was set. We added two delivery mechanisms to close these gaps. When a new interest is added to Interested In, the system sends an extra fetch request outside the normal fetch cycle, called a supplementary tail load, to retrieve fresh recommendations so matching content appears quickly. When an interest is added to Not Interested In, cache invalidation handles candidates ranked before the change. The client obtains the new interest’s clusters and drops any cached content that matches them before it is displayed. Figure 3: Where Your algorithm preferences act in the content ranking funnel. LLMs Across the Preference Lifecycle: From Profile to Final Check LLMs play a role at several key points in a preference’s life in Your algorithm. They generate the initial profile that people see on a first visit, validate each change as it is made, and give the final recommendations a last check against interests in Not Interested In (Figure 2). Each use comes with its own constraints, including latency, serving capacity, and safety, and evaluating them requires a new approach as well. Profile generation provides the starting content for a first visit: the inferred interests and the Lately Summary. An LLM turns interest signals, which are refreshed regularly, into a set of inferred interests with clear, readable topic names. These are prefilled in the Interested In list and reflect past viewing across Facebook Feed and Reels. The LLM also writes the Lately Summary, a sentence that highlights ongoing interests. Together, they provide a recognizable starting point that is easy to review and correct. Every edit on the Your algorithm page passes through preference management. When an interest is added or moved, an LLM checks that the phrase is a coherent topic, detects duplicates, and maps it to a clean topic name. This step runs on a smaller model that is efficient to serve at scale. The validated interest is then enriched with the signals ranking needs, such as an embedding and search keywords, and saved to the shared preference store. The LLM is only one layer of validation. The system also has a dedicated component that performs integrity and safety checks. Once recommendations are ranked, LLM reranking provides a last check against interests in Not Interested In. The ranking funnel matches interests to candidates using embeddings, which are fast but coarse. To catch what they miss, a fine-tuned LLM reviews the ranked list and removes content it judges to be related to an interest recently added to Not Interested In. A key insight was that a small model fine-tuned to return only the items to remove was faster and more reliable than a general-purpose model judging each item individually. Evaluating these LLM calls required its own approach. Standard offline metrics cannot tell whether a Lately Summary is accurate or whether the reranker removed the right candidates, so a separate LLM acts as a judge, grading each call’s output against expected behavior. This provides an objective, repeatable way to compare prompts and models before launch. The Future of Your Algorithm Your algorithm creates a more transparent and personalized recommendation experience, informed by both behavior and stated intent. But there are important opportunities remaining, such as better interpreting ambiguous input and making recommendations respond even more precisely to each request. We are also exploring additional entry points so that preferences can be shaped from more places.
